claims.text: The studied particles are sub-5 nm AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles produced by pulsed laser deposition on a silicon nitride membrane.
The FCC structure of the AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles is kinetically trapped rather than equilibrium-stabilized.
The initial nanoparticles have non-equilibrium elliptical or icosahedral shapes.
Surface-energy-minimization gradients override sluggish bulk diffusion in AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles during heating.
Bulk sluggish diffusion persists in the alloy because of high mixing entropy and lattice distortion.
Reduced atomic coordination at a nanoparticle surface lowers the surface-diffusion activation energy relative to the bulk-diffusion activation energy.
Surface diffusion coefficients exceed bulk diffusion coefficients by orders of magnitude in the relevant temperature regime.
Au and Cu have sufficiently low surface energies to preferentially segregate to the nanoparticle surface.
Au and Cu migrate to the surface to reduce the total Gibbs free energy of the nanoparticles.
The surface contribution to free energy dominates the bulk contribution for particles with radii or diameters below 10 nm.
Lower-melting-point elements can preferentially segregate relative to higher-melting-point elements.
Surface enrichment of Au and Cu creates a concentration gradient that drives their evaporation.
Loss of Au and Cu destabilizes the particles and causes coalescence of a remaining Pt- and Ni-rich refractory core.
The surface-driven mechanism becomes dominant at a critical temperature between 600 K and 800 K for sub-5 nm particles.
Above the critical temperature, Au/Cu surface segregation and evaporation proceed faster than bulk diffusion.
Above the critical temperature, the particle-size distribution widens, particles become spherical, and the smallest particles disappear.
Surface-energy gradients alone can reproduce the observed segregation profiles without treating bulk sluggish diffusion as the primary driver.
The proposed mechanism applies only below 10 nm and not to bulk alloys or larger nanoparticles.
Configurational entropy can stabilize an FCC phase at elevated temperature in a high-entropy alloy.
Thermal longitudinal spin fluctuations alter magnetic entropy and free energy in CoCrFeMnNi.
